Connect to foundations: Stars, gas, vacuum, and the forces of nature ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Shear can drive waves even at equal density Two fluids moving at different speeds along an interface can transfer bulk kinetic energy into interface waves. This is Kelvin–Helmholtz instability. RT uses density ordering relative to effective acceleration; KH is driven by shear. Use the RT chapter’s incompressible, inviscid, infinitely deep half-spaces, upper density ρ₁ and lower density ρ₂. Background velocities U₁ and U₂ are uniform and parallel to x, discontinuous at the interface. Initially set g = 0, with no surface tension or magnetic field and k > 0 parallel to the flow. Rewrite the RT chapter’s potential flow and pressure conditions to include advection. 02Use the frequency seen by each stream Following each stream changes the time derivative to ∂/∂t + Uj∂/∂x. Acting on ei(kx−ωt) gives −i(ω−kUj). Define this stream-relative frequency as Ωj. Ω₁ = ω−kU₁, Ω₂ = ω−kU₂ a₁ = iΩ₁ζ₀k, a₂ = −iΩ₂ζ₀k Pressure perturbations also use δpj = −ρj(∂/∂t + Uj∂/∂x)φj. Matching interface pressures gives, for g = 0: ρ₁(ω−kU₁)² + ρ₂(ω−kU₂)² = 0 03Complete the square to separate drift and growth Subtract the density-weighted mean velocity Ū and complete the square. With ΔU = U₁ − U₂: Ū ≡ ρ₁U₁+ρ₂U₂ρ₁+ρ₂ (ω−kŪ)² = −ρ₁ρ₂(ρ₁+ρ₂)²k²(ΔU)² ω = kŪ ± iσ, σ = √(ρ₁ρ₂)ρ₁+ρ₂k|ΔU| The pattern drifts at Ū while one branch grows as eσt. Equal densities still give σ = k|ΔU|/2. Adding the same velocity to both streams changes drift but not growth. Larger density contrast reduces growth at the same shear. 04Combine gravity and shear in one relation Restore the RT chapter’s downward g. Pressure matching becomes ρ₁Ω₁² + ρ₂Ω₂² = (ρ₂−ρ₁)gk. Completing the square again puts gravity and shear in a single relation. (ω−kŪ)² = −Agk − ρ₁ρ₂(ρ₁+ρ₂)²k²(ΔU)² A ≡ ρ₁−ρ₂ρ₁+ρ₂ A positive right-hand side gives advected oscillations; a negative value gives growing and decaying branches. For A > 0, RT and KH both destabilize. For A < 0, gravity supports long waves, but the shear term proportional to k² wins at sufficiently short wavelengths. A zero-thickness inviscid velocity jump has σ ∝ k and no finite fastest-growing wavelength. Finite shear thickness, compressibility, magnetic fields, and viscosity change this. The statement that all wavelengths are unstable applies here to the ideal g = 0 model. 05A linear wave is not a vortex simulation Wave roll-up, vortices, and mixing are nonlinear stages. Jets and surrounding gas or gas clouds moving at different speeds are applications, but their stability depends on actual density, sound speed, magnetic field, and velocity profiles. The panel draws a single linear mode of the derived dispersion relation, not a nonlinear fluid simulation. Comparing RT, KH, Jeans, and Toomre instabilities asks the same useful questions: what supplies energy, and what opposes the disturbance? CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. For equal densities, no gravity, ΔU = 2 m/s, and λ = 2π m, what is the growth rate? What happens if the wavelength halves? Does linear theory determine the eventual vortices? Show the answer and reasoning σ = k|ΔU|/2 = 1 s⁻¹. Halving the wavelength doubles k and σ. Linear theory describes initial small-amplitude growth; rolled-up vortices and mixing are nonlinear. An ideal zero-thickness interface without viscosity or another small-scale regulator has no finite fastest-growing wavelength.
